clue.text: Fail pious quest, regularly back boozing on this?

indicators.note: back tells the solver to read the kept letters from the end towards the start
regularly means taking every other letter, at a steady interval, from the words before it

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth letters and so on of these three words

explanation.surface: A drinker abandons a holy pilgrimage and returns to the bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: The even letters of 'Fail pious quest' read backwards spell TEQUILA; the question mark flags that the definition is a loose description rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Tequila is a Mexican spirit, the kind of drink someone might get drunk on.

clue.text: Defeat admitted in umpteenth war trial

indicators.note: admitted in says the letters are let inside the following words, sitting within them

parts.note: runs from the end of umpteenth through war to the start of trial

explanation.surface: A defeat is acknowledged during yet another war crimes trial.
explanation.definitionFit: To thwart a plan is to frustrate or block it, a verb sense of beating or foiling.

clue.text: Charity supporting Queen's misgivings

indicators.note: in a down clue, supporting puts one piece underneath the other, so it comes second

parts.note: QU is an abbreviation for queen
alms are charitable gifts to the poor

explanation.surface: A charity backed by royal patronage has some doubts.
explanation.definitionFit: Qualms are uneasy doubts or pangs of conscience, a close synonym for misgivings.

clue.text: Personally provided solver with invitation to quiz setter

parts.note: provided as a conjunction means on condition that
the setter addresses the solver as you
inviting someone to question the setter, who calls themself me

explanation.surface: A setter personally sends the solver an invitation to a quiz night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quiz' looks like a noun for a trivia event, but it is the verb to question.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase introduces a personal opinion, much as one says 'in my view' before stating it.

clue.text: Australian cricketers love maidens — that's self-evident

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for Australian
a cricket team has eleven players, written XI
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
M is the abbreviation for maiden overs on a cricket scorecard

explanation.surface: It is obvious the Australian cricket team loves bowling maiden overs.
explanation.walkthrough: A maiden in cricket is an over in which no runs are scored.
explanation.definitionFit: An axiom is a statement accepted as true without proof because it seems obvious.

clue.text: Unemployed chap, long-suffering? Not so much

parts.note: Job, the Bible figure famous for his patient suffering
less means a smaller amount

explanation.surface: An out-of-work man has suffered for ages, though perhaps not so badly.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone jobless has no paid work, the same state as being unemployed.

clue.text: Electricity suppliers bound to direct debits ultimately

parts.note: to bound is to leap
to direct is to lead

indicators.note: ultimately points to the very last letter of the word it follows

parts.note: the final letter of debits

explanation.surface: Energy companies are obliged to take payment by direct debit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Direct debits' reads as one banking phrase, but the words are split. Jump leads are the British name for jumper cables.
explanation.definitionFit: Jump leads are cables that carry power from one car battery to start another.

clue.text: Smell — dubiously at first — unknown substance

parts.note: BO is the standard abbreviation for an unpleasant personal odour

indicators.note: at first picks out only the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: the opening letter of dubiously
y is an unknown quantity in algebra

explanation.surface: A suspicious odour comes from some mysterious substance.
explanation.definitionFit: Body means substance in the sense of solidity or weight, as a wine with plenty of body.

clue.text: Turn up to decide a title for issues

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up flips the letters so they read from bottom to top

parts.note: to set a date is to decide it
taken as written
a title is a name

explanation.surface: Someone arrives to choose a headline for a run of magazine issues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issues' looks like a noun for editions, but it is the verb: comes out.
explanation.definitionFit: To emanate is to flow out from a source, as a sound or smell issues from somewhere.

clue.text: Observe Russia possibly recruiting muscle

indicators.note: recruiting means taking someone into the ranks, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Russia is an example of a nation
pec is short for pectoral muscle

explanation.surface: Watch as Russia enlists armed force.
explanation.definitionFit: To spectate is to watch an event as an onlooker rather than take part.

clue.text: Exhausted and inclined to blaspheme when losing head

indicators.note: losing its head means the word drops its first letter

parts.note: sweary is informal for given to swearing

explanation.surface: Someone is so tired they keep cursing, until they lose their temper.
explanation.definitionFit: Weary means tired out, very close in sense to exhausted.

clue.text: "Bard is average, limited and borders on third-rate" — that's direct!

indicators.note: limited means cut short, so the word before it loses its last letter

parts.note: Bard is this puzzle's setter, who says I am, shortened
the median is a kind of average

indicators.note: the borders of a word are its edges, its first and last letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of third-rate

explanation.surface: A critic bluntly calls the setter mediocre and close to third-rate.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter names themself, so 'Bard is' is I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: Immediate can mean direct, with nothing coming between, as in an immediate cause.

clue.text: Expose Trump, foul army and silly gossip mongers

indicators.note: to expose something is to strip off its covering, here the outside letters of each word

parts.note: Trump without its outer letters
foul without its outer letters
army without its outer letters
silly without its outer letters

explanation.surface: A campaign to reveal a politician's dirty army secrets spreads through the tabloids.
explanation.definitionFit: The rumour mill is the informal network of people who spread hearsay and tittle-tattle.

clue.text: Newspaper contains current information

indicators.note: contains says one piece holds the other inside it

parts.note: FT is the Financial Times
AC is alternating current

explanation.surface: A paper carries up-to-date news.
explanation.definitionFit: A fact is a piece of verified data, a single item of what is known.

clue.text: Seaside flats and ramshackle spa leased around November

indicators.note: around says the jumbled letters go about the next piece
something ramshackle is tumbledown and disordered, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
N is November in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Holiday apartments and a run-down spa are rented out in November.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flats' looks like apartments, but here it means level stretches of ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Esplanades are long level promenades along a seafront, so they are flat strips by the sea.

clue.text: Computer file parsed these incorrectly

indicators.note: done incorrectly means put together the wrong way, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A program has misread some data from a document.
explanation.definitionFit: A spreadsheet is a document of rows and columns kept on a computer, such as an Excel workbook.

clue.text: Quickly ran through dance with Sheeran in the wings

parts.note: a reel is a lively Scottish dance
Ed Sheeran, the British singer
a performer waiting in the wings is offstage

explanation.surface: A dancer performs while a pop star waits backstage.
explanation.definitionFit: To reel off a list is to recite it rapidly and fluently without pausing.

clue.text: Grammatically suspect description of history, so to speak

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read cryptically: history is how things were, said with 'it' and 'were' oddly paired
second meaning: a phrase softening a figurative remark

explanation.walkthrough: The first half pretends 'as it were' is bad grammar for 'as it was', which is what history describes.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is used to flag that words are meant loosely or metaphorically, just like 'so to speak'.

clue.text: Pupil's equipment not shading, their caps left off earlier

indicators.note: earlier puts the rearranged piece ahead of the other one
off means not right, so the word before it is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

indicators.note: the caps of words are their capital, or opening, letters

parts.note: the opening letters of these four words

explanation.surface: A schoolchild's kit isn't colouring properly because the lids were left off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pupil's equipment' does double duty: it is the definition, and its initials join those of 'not shading'.
explanation.definitionFit: Felt-tip pens are colouring pens that schoolchildren commonly use in class.

clue.text: Saves me almost crashing into metal ship

indicators.note: into says the jumbled letters go inside the next piece

parts.note: steel is an example of a metal

indicators.note: crashing suggests a smash that scatters things, so the letters are jumbled
almost means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be shortened

explanation.surface: A driver who narrowly avoids a crash into a metal barrier is relieved.
explanation.definitionFit: A steam vessel is a ship driven by steam power, such as a paddle steamer.

clue.text: Swinger using tips from trapeze artist, really zipping around now!

indicators.note: tips are the front ends of things, so the first letter of each word is kept

parts.words: trapeze artist, really zipping around now
parts.note: the opening letters of these six words

explanation.surface: An acrobat on the swing borrows tricks from a trapeze performer flying through the air.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarzan is the jungle hero of fiction who travels by swinging from vine to vine.

clue.text: Dull fare, e.g. peppers, thrown back up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going back up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
to pepper something is to dot or sprinkle it

explanation.surface: Someone vomits after a heavy meal containing peppers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peppers' looks like the vegetable, but it is the verb meaning sprinkles. Stodge is British for heavy, filling, starchy food.
explanation.definitionFit: Stodge is heavy, unexciting food, like stodgy puddings, so it is dull fare.

clue.text: Skirt unfashionable, unloved and sent back repeatedly

indicators.note: repeatedly means the piece is written out twice in a row
sent back means the letters are read from right to left
without love means the letter that looks like zero is taken out

parts.note: something out is no longer in fashion

explanation.surface: A dated, unwanted skirt keeps being returned to the shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Love is O, so OUT without love is UT.
explanation.definitionFit: A tutu is the short stiff skirt worn by a ballerina.

clue.text: Maybe grandchild can send Ted loopy

indicators.note: loopy means crazy, so the letters are put in a mad new order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A grandchild is able to drive Grandpa Ted round the bend.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandchild is one example of a descendant, someone in a later generation of a family line.

clue.text: Rib about 'big trap' occasionally

parts.note: c, short for circa, means about
OS is outsize, a clothing size for big

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter is kept

parts.note: the first and third letters of trap

explanation.surface: Someone teases another person now and then about their big mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rib' looks like the verb to tease, and 'big trap' like a big mouth; it is the Latin anatomical word for a rib.
explanation.definitionFit: Costa is the anatomical Latin term for a rib, used in medical words such as intercostal.

clue.text: Food to accompany 1A, served up by advocate

indicators.note: in a down clue, served up means the letters read from bottom to top
by here means held within, so the letters lie inside the next word

parts.note: the middle letters of advocate

explanation.surface: A lawyer serves Mexican snacks with the drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 1A is TEQUILA, a fellow Mexican item.
explanation.definitionFit: A taco is a Mexican folded tortilla with a filling, the sort of food eaten alongside tequila.

clue.text: Settle or else! Tax collected for public transport going up

indicators.note: collected means taken in, so one piece goes inside the other
to settle things is to put them in a new arrangement, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
VAT is value added tax

explanation.surface: A tax collector threatens a debtor to pay up or face consequences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Settle' looks like paying a bill, which fits the tax story, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Elevators, the American word for lifts, carry the public between floors upwards.

clue.text: How dimwit begins Observer puzzle — bewildered

indicators.note: how a word begins is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of dimwit
Azed is the long-running cryptic crossword in The Observer, a British Sunday paper

explanation.surface: A dim solver starts the notoriously hard Sunday crossword and is baffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Dazed means stunned and unable to think clearly, close to bewildered or confused.

clue.text: Relax in middle of Red Sea, swimming away

indicators.note: the middle of a short word is its central letter

parts.note: the central letter of Red

indicators.note: swimming suggests the letters are moving about and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
away means gone off

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker unwinds by swimming far out in the Red Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: To ease off is to slacken effort or loosen up, a phrasal verb for taking it easier.

clue.text: Deficiency spotted in Ahab's encephalogram

indicators.note: spotted in says the letters can be seen sitting inside the following words

parts.note: runs from the end of Ahab's into the start of encephalogram

explanation.surface: A doctor spots a defect in the brain scan of Captain Ahab, of Moby-Dick.
explanation.definitionFit: An absence is a lack of something, which is what a deficiency also describes.
